rationale: While checking whether the post-shutdown finding's release condition could be witnessed directly, I found that my saved premise was too generous about who releases the parked caller. The network transport's response wait selects on the transport's own shutdown channel as well as the response channel, so closing that transport releases the waiter; but the in-memory transport's Close does nothing except disconnect - it never closes the shutdown channel the transport's field holds - so with that transport there is no release signal at all, and an accepted heartbeat after the node is down is not merely unanswered for a while, it is never answered. The observed receipt for this question is unchanged and still the target of its experiment: the post-shutdown delivery received nothing within the bound while the term stayed put, and the live control was answered. What changes is the account of the escape, so I correct the behaviour entry on its existing id rather than restating it as if it were new, add the two source ranges that settle it, and record the corrected account as the question's current interpretation over the same receipt. No execution is needed for a claim about which close path signals what, and I am not spending one.

knowledge.statement: processHeartbeat begins by checking the node's shutdown channel and returning immediately when it is closed, before it inspects the command and before appendEntries runs, and that branch never calls Respond. On the fast path the transport has already handed the request to the handler and is waiting on the response channel it supplied, and whether that waiter is ever released depends on the transport: the network transport's wait also selects on the transport's own shutdown channel, which its Close signals, while the in-memory transport's Close only disconnects its peers and never closes the shutdown channel it created, so with that transport nothing releases the waiter.
knowledge.conditions: This revision, any transport that installs the heartbeat handler and any node whose shutdown channel is closed while the transport is still open. The release path is transport-supplied: NetworkTransport's Close signals the channel its response wait selects on, InmemTransport's Close does not signal its shutdown channel at all, and Raft.Shutdown's future closes the transport only when the caller waits on it.
knowledge.changed_premise: The premise changes in one respect: the earlier statement treated the transport's shutdown channel as the waiter's escape and the closure of the transport as what releases it, without distinguishing transports. The network transport does provide that escape, but the in-memory transport's Close only disconnects and never closes its shutdown channel, so for that transport the accepted heartbeat has no release at all - the caller is not merely delayed until a close, it is never woken. The observed receipt is unaffected and still supports the finding; only the account of the escape is narrowed to the transport that implements one. The saved use that relied on the earlier phrasing is the interpretation at operation a3e037c016ac4e2f976d62b3165916ce, which stays valid because its operands are unchanged and only the release condition is corrected.

interpretations.rationale: The receipt still carries the finding unchanged: delivered while the node was live and top of term, the fast-path heartbeat was answered successfully and moved the term; delivered again after Shutdown with the transport left open, it received nothing within the bound and the term stayed put, so the handler returned at its shutdown check before running the term logic and nothing responded. What this turn corrects is the escape I had described as bounding the harm. The network transport's response wait selects on the response channel and on the transport's own shutdown channel, so a caller waiting on behalf of that transport is released when the transport is closed - and Raft.Shutdown's future closes it when the caller waits on the future. The in-memory transport has no such path: its Close disconnects its peers and returns, leaving the shutdown channel it created unclosed, so a waiter parked on the same code path through that transport is never released at all. That makes the finding sharper for one transport family and narrower for the other rather than changing it: the duty is accepted and then has no completion path, with the only difference being whether some transport eventually abandons the waiter with a transport-shutdown error or leaves it parked forever. Since this is a claim about which close path signals what, source settles it and no execution is warranted; I reused the existing receipt rather than rerunning it, and corrected the behaviour entry on its existing id so the saved premise no longer overstates the release.
counterevidence: The correction narrows rather than widens the earlier account on one transport and widens it on the other; it does not change the observed operands, which came from the harness wrapper that mirrors the network transport's dispatch.
The in-memory transport's lack of a close signal is its own behaviour and is not a defect of the fast path; it matters here because it removes the release the finding's earlier phrasing assumed.

The parked caller is still the heartbeat path for a peer that is already gone from the cluster's perspective, so the cluster-level consequence remains a stalled per-peer delivery rather than anything about agreement or commit.
limitations: Still one execution for the observation; the transport-specific release conditions are read from source rather than measured on each transport.

The harness wrapper mirrors the network transport's wait, including its shutdown escape, so the in-memory transport's missing signal is a property of the underlying transport rather than something this execution exercised.
